Thesis watch

A dated analysis note reads the whole page together and names the readings that would prove it wrong. They are checked here on every refresh.

Holds · US card credit is re-segmenting, not cycling: the 2022-24 loss surge was a vintage event, and the repricing that came with it is structural. Stated 2026-09-08 in design/thesis-2026-09-08.html.
  • ✓ Flow into 90+ day delinquency stays below 7.5%: 6.97% in 2026 Q2. A break above this would mean the loosening that began in late 2025 was larger than the small line sizes suggest, and that this is a cycle after all.
  • ✓ Card charge-off rate stays below 4.2%: 3.82% in 2026 Q2. Losses reaccelerating while unemployment is near 4% would break the argument that the surge was a vintage event that has washed out.
  • ✓ Card APR margin over prime stays above 14 points: 15.40 pp in 2026 Q2. The margin falling back toward its 2015-19 level of 10.7 points would mean the repricing was cyclical, not structural.

Plain-text version of these readings and the thesis watch, for pasting into a post. Charts open on the last 5 years; the button on each card shows the full history. Shaded bands are NBER recessions.

Growth

How much card credit is outstanding, how fast it is growing, and who holds it.

Pricing

What card borrowers are charged, and what issuers advertise.

Access

Who is asking for card credit, who is getting it, and who is being shut out. The demand side, from the only survey that asks households directly.

Performance

How card credit on lenders' books is performing, and whether banks are tightening.

Borrowers

How households are using and servicing card credit, and who is getting new cards.

Distribution

Who owes the consumer credit and what stands behind it: the Fed's household balance sheet by wealth, income and age.

Spend

What the cards are buying: household spending and retail sales by category, and how card purchase volume tracks them.

Context

What the card numbers sit inside: the cost of household debt, the buffer behind it, and how people say they feel.

    Data and method

    • Download every series as one CSV (metric, entity, tier, period_end, period_type, value, source, pulled_at).
    • Every period is dated to its last day: month end, quarter end, or the Wednesday for weekly bank data. A quarterly survey taken in May is shown at June 30; the July Senior Loan Officer survey, which asks about the quarter just ended, is shown at June 30.
    • Step charts hold each reading across its own period. Nothing is interpolated between readings. Charts open on the last 5 years; the button on each card shows the full history.
    • Shaded bands are NBER recessions (peak month to trough month). Dashed grey lines are the 2015-2019 average of the first series on the chart, the last full expansion before the pandemic.
    • SA means seasonally adjusted. Series are labeled SA or NSA and are never compared across that line.
    • Different sources measure different populations. G.19 covers all lenders; the H.8, charge-off and APR series cover commercial banks only; the Y-14 series cover the largest banks; the NY Fed series are credit reports, all lenders; the FDIC series are bank charters. Notes under each chart say which, with a link to the source.
    • "Data as of" on a chart is when its newest value was loaded. A card carries a status badge when its source is not OK; "last fetch attempt" is then the run that failed. "Checked against the release" lists the numbers the pipeline reproduces from the source's own release page on every run.
    • The latest readings are computed from the series on the page: latest value, change against the same period a year earlier, the 2015-2019 average for rates, and whether the value is the highest or lowest in at least three years. No model writes any of it.
    • Sources: Federal Reserve Board, via FRED; CFPB Terms of Credit Card Plans survey; Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia, Large Bank Credit Card and Mortgage Data (FR Y-14M); Federal Reserve Bank of New York, Quarterly Report on Household Debt and Credit (Consumer Credit Panel/Equifax); FDIC, Call Report data via the BankFind Suite API; Federal Reserve Bank of New York, Survey of Consumer Expectations Credit Access Survey; Federal Reserve Bank of New York, Survey of Consumer Expectations (monthly); Bureau of Economic Analysis, personal consumption expenditures by type of product (NIPA monthly); Census Bureau, Monthly Retail Trade Survey; NCUA, 5300 Call Report quarterly data (credit unions); Federal Reserve Board, Distributional Financial Accounts; CFPB Consumer Credit Trends (Consumer Credit Panel); Capital One Financial Corporation, monthly charge-off and delinquency metrics (8-K Exhibit 99.1, SEC EDGAR); Federal Reserve Bank of New York, State Level Household Debt Statistics (Consumer Credit Panel/Equifax). The Federal Reserve Board series (G.19 Consumer Credit, H.8 Assets and Liabilities of Commercial Banks, Charge-Off and Delinquency Rates, Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey) are retrieved from FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis.
    • A dated analysis note reading the whole page together, with the numbers behind it and the test that would prove it wrong, is at design/thesis-2026-09-08.html (also in the repository). The page above is mechanical; that note is editorial and dated.
    • Every chart is also written as a PNG (the link in its footer), drawn from the same data as the page and showing the same 5-year window. The image carries no pull date, so it changes only when the data does.
    • "Expected around" under each source is the period after the newest one loaded, plus the lag its releases have shown; it is a reader's expectation, not a status. The loader marks a source stale on its own rule.
